findings.text: Early platform setup discovers one hypervisor and, when one is found, installs its non empty initialization and runtime hooks into generic tables, records the selected type in a global, and invokes the installed platform initializer; with no hypervisor it returns without side effects.

Vendor detection walks the built in table in order, skips entries that do not opt out when the no paravirt flag is set, asks each remaining entry for a priority, keeps the highest positive priority entry, logs its name when present, and returns null when none claims the platform.

The hypervisor table is a fixed init time array of pointers to vendor descriptors with unconditional entries for common hypervisors and additional entries included only when corresponding guest support is configured.
Hook installation copies pointer sized slots from source to target and only overwrites target slots where the source slot is non null, leaving other generic slots unchanged.
A kernel command line switch sets a global flag that disables paravirtual hypervisor detection except for vendors that explicitly ignore the flag.
The lane exposes a global recording the detected hypervisor type, an early initialization routine for hypervisor platform setup, and a global no paravirt flag consumed during detection.

Cyrix configuration sequences that toggle extended map access save and disable local interrupts, preserve unrelated control bits while enabling map access, perform indexed register updates, restore the prior map control value, then restore interrupt state.

On family three parts the SLOP check inspects a status bit under map access; when set it clears that bit, restores map state, logs recalibration, reruns delay calibration, and propagates the refreshed loops value into the per CPU record.

Reorder setup enables map access, clears a serialize disable in a performance control register, and widens a serialize range in map control; write back setup unlocks a cache control bit, requests not write through through control register zero, then relocks and sets related cache bits.

Geode configuration runs with interrupts disabled, enables halt related power saving, enables map access to set fast floating point plus cache and bypass options, disables map access again, then applies write back and reorder setups before restoring interrupts.

Early Cyrix setup reads device identification, derives a family code from the upper half of the first identifier, and marks address range register emulation for the two mid generation families that need MTRR like behavior.

Cyrix initialization remaps a legacy feature bit to a Cyrix multimedia bit, refreshes device identifiers, runs the SLOP check, derives family from the upper nibble and multiplier from the lower nibble, derives model and stepping from the second identifier, and composes a printable model string from a family table plus an optional suffix.

Per family handling selects naming and multiplier tables, enables address range emulation and a coma bug flag on affected generations, sets cache size and multimedia enable on MediaGX and Geode paths, invokes Geode tuning for defined identifier ranges, and distinguishes M II from older MX by a stepping threshold.

MediaGX and Geode handling unconditionally marks the ISA DMA bridge as buggy for audio workarounds and, when the companion PCI vendor and device match two listed Cyrix bridge models, marks the time stamp counter unstable.

Cyrix detection on family four uses flags behavior after a small integer divide to recognize parts with CPUID disabled, records a Cyrix vendor identity, rereads identifiers, and for two affected families enables map access to set a CPUID enable bit under interrupt protection.

Two static CPU device records publish vendor names and match strings with Cyrix binding early, full, and identify hooks and NSC binding only a full initialization hook, each tagged with its vendor identifier.
NSC initialization handles one GX generation locally by detecting cache sizes and delegates every other processor to the shared Cyrix initialization path.

Debug filesystem setup creates a topology directory with a domains file and a per possible CPU subdirectory where each CPU file is bound to its numeric identifier; open handlers connect these files to single open sequence display routines.

Per CPU display reports online state and, when initialized, APIC and topology identifiers plus package hierarchy and system wide thread core and die limits; domain display iterates all topology domains accumulating thread counts while showing shift, size, and accumulated thread values with fixed domain labels.
Both debug files use sequence file operations where open uses single open, read and seek use sequence helpers, and release uses single release.
A global helper translates an internal CPU type enumeration into a stable lowercase name with a fallback name for unrecognized types.
Virtualization feature leaf enumeration defines six ordered positions covering miscellaneous features, primary controls, secondary controls, tertiary low, tertiary high, and a terminal count.
A no SGX boot option clears the SGX capability during early init and reports successful parsing.
Messages from the feature control file share a common x86 CPU log prefix.
Nearby node lookup scans APIC to node mappings downward from the given identifier for the closest online node, then upward when none is found below, and finally falls back to the first online node.

Hygon NUMA placement prefers the current CPU node assignment, falls back to last level cache identity, applies an optional platform fixup, and when offline resolves through an initial APIC based mapping or nearby search before recording the result for the current CPU.

Hygon early setup marks a legacy K8 capability, snapshots microcode level, derives constant and nonstop TSC plus power and RAPL capabilities from power leaf bits, and unconditionally enables syscall and virtual machine call related capabilities with extended APIC identifier handling on capable builds.

Hygon full initialization reruns early setup, marks repeat string, Zen, cache partitioning, and always running APIC timer capabilities, sizes caches, resolves NUMA placement, initializes cache info, disables virtualization when firmware reports it disabled, enables load fence serialization and its timestamp protection on capable parts, and adjusts system return and fence behavior.

Hygon boot processor setup warns when constant TSC hardware state suggests firmware misconfiguration, selects a monitor wait delay implementation when supported, opportunistically enables speculative store bypass defenses from a configuration MSR without faulting, and invokes resource control detection.

Hygon TLB sizing requires a minimum extended level, reads data and instruction sizes from a later extended leaf, falls back to an earlier leaf when second level entries are disabled, and derives four megabyte counts as half the corresponding two megabyte counts.
A static Hygon device record publishes vendor and match identity and binds early, TLB, boot processor, and full initialization hooks with its vendor tag.
Self snoop capability is cleared on a fixed list of older Yonah, Merom, Penryn, Dunnington, Nehalem, Westmere, and SandyBridge model identifiers.

Ring three monitor wait is enabled only on family six Xeon Phi accelerator models unless disabled by a boot switch; when enabled it sets a CPU capability and a per CPU shadow bit and, on the boot processor, also sets a user visible hardware capability.
A boot option records that ring three monitor wait must stay disabled and reports that it consumed the option.
